expectedText:
EMPLOYER-REQUIRED CASH BONDS, DEPOSITS, AND PHOTOGRAPHS (LABOR CODE §§ 400–410) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Route Sales, Inc.

ABOUT THIS EMPLOYEE CASH BOND AND PHOTOGRAPH INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes Article 2 (Bonds and Photographs) of Chapter 3 of Part 1 of Division 2 of the California Labor Code, Sections 400 through 410, which governs an employer's demand for or acceptance of a cash bond, deposit, or other property from an employee or job applicant, allocates the cost of any bond or photograph an employer requires, treats disguised deposits (notes, loans, or investments tied to employment) as bonds, declares investments or stock purchases made in connection with securing a position contrary to public policy, and provides criminal penalties and Labor Commissioner enforcement. Acme Route Sales, Inc. has described its practices, if any, regarding bonds, deposits, photographs, or investments required of employees or applicants as follows: Route drivers who take consigned merchandise are asked to post a $500 deposit; no photographs or investments are required. This document states the content of the statutes and of published case law as of the date checked; it does not determine whether any particular payment, deposit, or arrangement is a "bond" within the meaning of the article or whether either statutory exception applies, and it is not a substitute for individualized legal advice or for consulting a licensed attorney.

THE ARTICLE APPLIES TO JOB APPLICANTS AS WELL AS EMPLOYEES
Labor Code Section 400 defines "applicant," as used in Article 2 (Bonds and Photographs), to mean an applicant for employment. The operative provisions of the article that follow — on the cost of bonds and photographs, the demand for or acceptance of a cash bond, the deposit and return of bond money, and the treatment of property put up as part of a contract of employment — refer to "employee or applicant," so the article's protections reach a person who has applied for a job as well as a person already employed.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "As used in this article, “applicant” means an applicant for employment."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 400, Lab. Code § 400 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=400.)
  Known gap: Section 400 defines only the term "applicant"; the article does not itself define "employer," "employee," or "bond," and this clause does not determine how those terms are construed. The statement that the operative provisions refer to "employee or applicant" summarizes the wording of Sections 401 through 406 as quoted in the other clauses of this document.

COST OF A REQUIRED BOND OR PHOTOGRAPH FALLS ON THE EMPLOYER
Under Labor Code Section 401, if an employer requires a bond or a photograph of an employee or applicant, the cost of the bond or photograph is to be paid by the employer.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "If a bond or photograph of an employee or applicant is required by any employer, the cost thereof shall be paid by the employer."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 401, Lab. Code § 401 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=401.)
  Known gap: Section 401 allocates cost only; it does not itself state whether or when an employer may require a bond or photograph, and it does not define "bond." Separate restrictions on demanding a cash bond appear in Section 402, addressed in another clause of this document. This clause does not address Labor Code Sections 1051 through 1054, which separately restrict an employer's use of fingerprints and photographs and are covered elsewhere in the corpus.

CASH BONDS MAY NOT BE DEMANDED OR ACCEPTED EXCEPT IN TWO SITUATIONS
Labor Code Section 402 provides that no employer may demand, exact, or accept any cash bond from any employee or applicant unless one of two conditions is met: (a) the employee or applicant is entrusted with property of an equivalent value, or (b) the employer regularly advances goods, wares, or merchandise to the employee for delivery or sale, for which the employer is reimbursed by the employee at regular periodic intervals, and the employer limits the cash bond to an amount sufficient to cover the value of the goods, wares, or merchandise advanced during the period before payment for them.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "No employer shall demand, exact, or accept any cash bond from any employee or applicant unless:"
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 402, Lab. Code § 402 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=402.)
  "The employee or applicant is entrusted with property of an equivalent value, or"
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 402(a), Lab. Code § 402(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=402.)
  "The employer advances regularly to the employee goods, wares, or merchandise to be delivered or sold by the employee, and for which the employer is reimbursed by the employee at regular periodic intervals, and the employer limits the cash bond to an amount sufficient to cover the value of the goods, wares, or merchandise so advanced during the period prior to the payment therefor."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 402(b), Lab. Code § 402(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=402.)
  Known gap: Section 402 governs cash bonds specifically; bonds in the form of other property are addressed by Sections 405 and 406 (separate clauses). The statute does not define "equivalent value" or state how it is measured, and this clause does not determine whether any particular arrangement satisfies exception (a) or (b).

CASH BONDS MUST BE DEPOSITED IN A JOINT-SIGNATURE SAVINGS ACCOUNT UNDER A WRITTEN AGREEMENT
Labor Code Section 403 requires that cash received as a bond be deposited in a savings account in a bank authorized to do business in California, withdrawable only upon the joint signatures of the employer and the employee or applicant. The statute further requires that cash put up as a bond be accompanied by a written agreement between the employer and the employee or applicant setting forth the conditions under which the bond is given.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "If cash is received as a bond it shall be deposited in a savings account in a bank authorized to do business in this State, and may be withdrawn only upon the joint signatures of the employer and the employee or applicant."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 403, Lab. Code § 403 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=403.)
  "Cash put up as a bond shall be accompanied by an agreement in writing made by the employer and employee or applicant, setting forth the conditions under which the bond is given."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 403, Lab. Code § 403 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=403.)
  Known gap: Section 403 does not specify the contents of the written agreement beyond "the conditions under which the bond is given," does not state who holds the passbook or account records, and does not address whether the account must be interest-bearing (Section 404's reference to "accrued interest" is quoted in a separate clause). The statute's phrase "in this State" is preserved as written.

BOND MONEY IS SHIELDED FROM THIRD-PARTY JUDGMENTS AND MUST BE RETURNED WITH INTEREST
Under Labor Code Section 404, money put up as a bond under Sections 401, 402, and 403 is not subject to enforcement of a money judgment except in an action between the employer and the employee or applicant (or their successors or assigns). The money, together with accrued interest, must be returned to the employee or applicant immediately upon the return of the money or property entrusted to the employee or applicant and upon fulfillment of the agreement, subject only to the deduction necessary to balance accounts between the employer and the employee or applicant.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "Any money put up as a bond under Sections 401, 402 and 403:"
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 404, Lab. Code § 404 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=404.)
  "Is not subject to enforcement of a money judgment except in an action between the employer and the employee or applicant, or their successors or assigns."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 404(a), Lab. Code § 404(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=404.)
  "Shall be returned to the employee or applicant together with accrued interest thereon, immediately upon the return of the money or property entrusted to the employee or applicant and upon the fulfillment of the agreement, subject only to the deduction necessary to balance accounts between the employer and employee or applicant."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 404(b), Lab. Code § 404(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=404.)
  Known gap: Section 404 does not define what deductions are "necessary to balance accounts," does not fix a time limit for return beyond "immediately," and does not address the interaction of that deduction with the wage-deduction limits of Labor Code Sections 221 through 224, which are not covered in this document.

BOND PROPERTY IS HELD IN TRUST; MISAPPROPRIATION OR COMMINGLING IS THEFT
Labor Code Section 405 provides that any property put up by an employee or applicant as a bond may not be used for any purpose other than liquidating accounts between the employer and employee or return to the employee or applicant, and must be held in trust for that purpose and not mingled with the employer's property. No contract between the employer and the employee or applicant can abrogate this section. An employer or prospective employer, or an agent or officer of one, who misappropriates such property, mingles it with their own, or uses it for any other purpose is guilty of theft and is punishable under the Penal Code provisions relating to theft.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "Any property put up by any employee or applicant as a bond shall not be used for any purpose other than liquidating accounts between the employer and employee or for return to the employee or applicant and shall be held in trust for this purpose and not mingled with the property of the employer."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 405, Lab. Code § 405 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=405.)
  "No contract between the employer and employee or applicant shall abrogate the provisions of this section."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 405, Lab. Code § 405 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=405.)
  "Any employer or prospective employer, or agent or officer thereof, who misappropriates any such property, mingles it with his own, or uses it for any other purpose than that herein set forth is guilty of theft and shall be punished in accordance with the provisions of the Penal Code relating to theft."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 405, Lab. Code § 405 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=405.)
  Known gap: Section 405 refers to "the provisions of the Penal Code relating to theft" without specifying a particular Penal Code section or grade of offense; the applicable theft classification and punishment (for example, the petty/grand theft distinction under Penal Code Sections 486 through 490) are not restated in this document. The statute's phrase "his own" is preserved as written in the quoted text.

PROPERTY PUT UP AS A NOTE, LOAN, OR INVESTMENT IS TREATED AS A BOND REGARDLESS OF LABELING
Labor Code Section 406 provides that any property put up by an employee or applicant as part of the contract of employment, directly or indirectly, is deemed to be put up as a bond and is subject to Article 2, whether the property is put up on a note, as a loan, or as an investment, and regardless of the wording of the agreement under which it is put up.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "Any property put up by an employee, or applicant as a part of the contract of employment, directly or indirectly, shall be deemed to be put up as a bond and is subject to the provisions of this article whether the property is put up on a note or as a loan or an investment and regardless of the wording of the agreement under which it is put up."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 406, Lab. Code § 406 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=406.)
  Known gap: Section 406 does not define "as a part of the contract of employment" or "directly or indirectly," and this clause does not determine whether any particular loan, note, or investment by a worker was put up as part of a contract of employment.

INVESTMENTS OR STOCK PURCHASES TIED TO SECURING A JOB ARE AGAINST PUBLIC POLICY
Labor Code Section 407 declares that investments and the sale of stock or an interest in a business in connection with the securing of a position are illegal as against the public policy of the State, and that they may not be advertised or held out in any way as part of the consideration for any employment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "Investments and the sale of stock or an interest in a business in connection with the securing of a position are illegal as against the public policy of the State and shall not be advertised or held out in any way as a part of the consideration for any employment."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 407, Lab. Code § 407 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=407.)
  Known gap: Section 407 does not itself define "in connection with the securing of a position," does not state whether a genuinely separate investment by a person who also becomes an employee is covered, and does not address employer equity-compensation programs offered after hire; this clause does not resolve those questions.

CRIMINAL PENALTIES, DISPOSITION OF FINES, AND LABOR COMMISSIONER ENFORCEMENT
Under Labor Code Section 408, any person, or agent or officer of a person, who violates any provision of Article 2 other than Section 405 is guilty of a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of not less than $50 and not more than $1,000, or imprisonment for not more than six months, or both. Section 409 directs that all fines imposed and collected under the article be paid into the State treasury and credited to the general fund. Section 410 assigns enforcement of the article to the Labor Commissioner.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "Any person or agent or officer thereof, who violates any provision of this article, except the provisions of Section 405, is guilty of a misdemeanor, punishable by a fine of not less than fifty dollars ($50) and not exceeding one thousand dollars ($1,000), or imprisonment for not exceeding six months, or both."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 408, Lab. Code § 408 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=408.)
  "All fines imposed and collected under this article shall be paid into the State treasury and credited to the general fund."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 409, Lab. Code § 409 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=409.)
  "The Labor Commissioner shall enforce this article."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 410, Lab. Code § 410 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=410.)
  Known gap: Section 408 excepts Section 405 because a violation of that section is punished as theft under the Penal Code (see the separate clause on Section 405). Article 2 does not itself create an express private right of action or a civil penalty, and this clause does not address whether or how an employee or applicant may recover bond money through a Labor Commissioner wage claim or a civil action; it also does not address the Labor Code Private Attorneys General Act.

CASE LAW: A 'BONUS' REDUCED BY CASH AND MERCHANDISE SHORTAGES CONTRAVENES THE BOND STATUTES
In Quillian v. Lion Oil Co. (1979), the California Court of Appeal affirmed a wage judgment for a service station manager whose monthly incentive bonus was calculated by subtracting the stations' cash and merchandise shortages from a sales-based figure. Relying on the California Supreme Court's decision in Kerr's Catering Service v. Department of Industrial Relations (1962), the court quoted that decision's description of Labor Code Sections 400 through 410 as setting out in detail the employee's bond law and the manner in which a cash bond may be exacted from an employee to cover merchandise entrusted to the employee. The court characterized the employer's calculation method as a clever method of circumventing the statutory definition of wages, concluded that the bonus was in contravention of the public policy expressed in Sections 400 to 410 pertaining to cash bonds that may be required of employees, and stated that because Section 408 attaches a criminal penalty, the imposition of the penalty implies a prohibition of the act and a contract provision founded upon such an act is void.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "Labor Code sections 400 through 410 set out in detail the employee’s bond law, and the manner in which a cash bond may be exacted from an employee to cover merchandise entrusted to him."
  — Quillian v. Lion Oil Co., 96 Cal. App. 3d 156, 162 (1979) (quoting Kerr's Catering Service v. Department of Industrial Relations, 57 Cal. 2d 319, 327-328 (1962)) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2110756/quillian-v-lion-oil-company/)
  "It appears to this court that this is merely a clever method of circumventing the statutory definition of wages."
  — Quillian v. Lion Oil Co., 96 Cal. App. 3d 156, 163 (1979) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2110756/quillian-v-lion-oil-company/)
  "Therefore, we conclude that the bonus herein is in contravention of the public policy expressed in sections 400 to 410 of the Labor Code pertaining to cash bonds that may be required of employees."
  — Quillian v. Lion Oil Co., 96 Cal. App. 3d 156, 163 (1979) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2110756/quillian-v-lion-oil-company/)
  "Accordingly, the imposition by statute of a penalty implies a prohibition of the act referred to and a contract provision founded upon such act is void."
  — Quillian v. Lion Oil Co., 96 Cal. App. 3d 156, 163 (1979) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2110756/quillian-v-lion-oil-company/)
  Known gap: Quillian involved shortages that were stipulated not to result from the employee's willful misconduct, dishonesty, or gross negligence; the opinion does not decide whether a different result would follow for losses caused by such conduct, and this clause does not address that question. The decision also rests on Labor Code Section 221 and the wage-deduction principles of Kerr's Catering, which are not separately covered in this document. The first quotation below is the Court of Appeal's reproduction of language from Kerr's Catering Service v. Department of Industrial Relations, 57 Cal.2d 319, 327-328 (1962), quoted as it appears in the Quillian opinion; the underlying Kerr's Catering opinion was not separately fetched for this document.

CASE LAW: A VOLUNTARY TRAINING-COST REIMBURSEMENT AGREEMENT WAS NOT A BOND
In USS-POSCO Industries v. Case (2016), the California Court of Appeal held that an agreement under which an employee who voluntarily enrolled in an employer-sponsored training program promised to repay a prorated share of program costs if he quit within 30 months of completing it did not violate the employee bond statutes. The court reasoned that Section 401 applies only to bonds an employer requires, that Section 402 prohibits demanding, exacting, or accepting a cash bond for most purposes, and that although a cash bond can take many forms under Section 406, the employee had put up no cash; the employer had fronted the training expenses and no deduction was ever made from the employee's paid wages. The court distinguished Quillian v. Lion Oil Co. as concerning a reduction in wages in the amount of a business shortage, a scenario it described as entirely different.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "For similar reasons, there was no violation of the statutes pertaining to employee bonds. Section 401 requires employers to pay for bonds if they are “required,” and so does not apply here. Section 402 prohibits the demanding, exacting, or accepting of any “cash bond” for most purposes. While a cash bond can take many forms (§ 406), here Case put up no cash. Rather, it was UPI that fronted his training expenses, and no deduction was ever made from his paid wages."
  — USS-POSCO Industries v. Case, 244 Cal. App. 4th 197, 207 (2016) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/3172339/uss-posco-industries-v-floyd-case/)
  "That case concerned a reduction in wages in the amount of a business shortage, a scenario entirely different from that here."
  — USS-POSCO Industries v. Case, 244 Cal. App. 4th 197, 207 (2016) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/3172339/uss-posco-industries-v-floyd-case/)
  Known gap: USS-POSCO also addressed the reimbursement agreement under Labor Code Sections 450, 2802, 221 through 223, and 432.5, Business and Professions Code Section 16600, and the federal Fair Labor Standards Act, and separately decided an attorney-fee question under Labor Code Section 218.5; none of those holdings is restated in this document. The decision turned on the program being voluntary and on the absence of any cash put up by the employee or deducted from wages; this clause does not determine how a mandatory training program, or a repayment obligation collected from wages, would be treated.

This information sheet regarding California Labor Code Sections 400 through 410 (employer-required bonds, deposits, photographs, and investments tied to employment) was prepared by Jordan T. Reyes for Acme Route Sales, Inc. and reviewed in Sacramento, California on September 10, 2026. It reflects the statutory and case-law text as of the date checked above and does not reflect any amendments or decisions issued after that date, and it is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney.

Department of Industrial Relations (1962), the court quoted that decision's description of Labor Code Sections 400 through 410 as setting out in detail the employee's bond law and the manner in which a cash bond may be exacted from an employee to cover merchandise entrusted to the employee. The court characterized the employer's calculation method as a clever method of circumventing the statutory definition of wages, concluded that the bonus was in contravention of the public policy expressed in Sections 400 to 410 pertaining to cash bonds that may be required of employees, and stated that because Section 408 attaches a criminal penalty, the imposition of the penalty implies a prohibition of the act and a contract provision founded upon such an act is void.

citations.cite: 96 Cal. App. 3d 156, 162 (1979) (quoting Kerr's Catering Service v. Department of Industrial Relations, 57 Cal. 2d 319, 327-328 (1962))
citations.quote: Labor Code sections 400 through 410 set out in detail the employee’s bond law, and the manner in which a cash bond may be exacted from an employee to cover merchandise entrusted to him.
It appears to this court that this is merely a clever method of circumventing the statutory definition of wages.
Therefore, we conclude that the bonus herein is in contravention of the public policy expressed in sections 400 to 410 of the Labor Code pertaining to cash bonds that may be required of employees.
Accordingly, the imposition by statute of a penalty implies a prohibition of the act referred to and a contract provision founded upon such act is void.

expectedJSON.gap: Quillian involved shortages that were stipulated not to result from the employee's willful misconduct, dishonesty, or gross negligence; the opinion does not decide whether a different result would follow for losses caused by such conduct, and this clause does not address that question. The decision also rests on Labor Code Section 221 and the wage-deduction principles of Kerr's Catering, which are not separately covered in this document. The first quotation below is the Court of Appeal's reproduction of language from Kerr's Catering Service v. Department of Industrial Relations, 57 Cal.2d 319, 327-328 (1962), quoted as it appears in the Quillian opinion; the underlying Kerr's Catering opinion was not separately fetched for this document.

expectedJSON.body: In USS-POSCO Industries v. Case (2016), the California Court of Appeal held that an agreement under which an employee who voluntarily enrolled in an employer-sponsored training program promised to repay a prorated share of program costs if he quit within 30 months of completing it did not violate the employee bond statutes. The court reasoned that Section 401 applies only to bonds an employer requires, that Section 402 prohibits demanding, exacting, or accepting a cash bond for most purposes, and that although a cash bond can take many forms under Section 406, the employee had put up no cash; the employer had fronted the training expenses and no deduction was ever made from the employee's paid wages. The court distinguished Quillian v. Lion Oil Co. as concerning a reduction in wages in the amount of a business shortage, a scenario it described as entirely different.

citations.quote: For similar reasons, there was no violation of the statutes pertaining to employee bonds. Section 401 requires employers to pay for bonds if they are “required,” and so does not apply here. Section 402 prohibits the demanding, exacting, or accepting of any “cash bond” for most purposes. While a cash bond can take many forms (§ 406), here Case put up no cash. Rather, it was UPI that fronted his training expenses, and no deduction was ever made from his paid wages.
That case concerned a reduction in wages in the amount of a business shortage, a scenario entirely different from that here.

expectedJSON.gap: USS-POSCO also addressed the reimbursement agreement under Labor Code Sections 450, 2802, 221 through 223, and 432.5, Business and Professions Code Section 16600, and the federal Fair Labor Standards Act, and separately decided an attorney-fee question under Labor Code Section 218.5; none of those holdings is restated in this document. The decision turned on the program being voluntary and on the absence of any cash put up by the employee or deducted from wages; this clause does not determine how a mandatory training program, or a repayment obligation collected from wages, would be treated.
